Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $H$ be a locally
square-integrable predictable process with energy process $A$ and canonical
localization times (indexed by $n\ge1$) $\tau_n=\inf\{t:A_t\ge n\}\wedge n$
[[def-locally-square-integrable-predictable-brownian-integrand]], and let
$M^{(n)}$ denote the continuous version of the finite-energy integral
$\int H1_{(0,\tau_n]}\,dB$
[[thm-ito-integral-process-has-a-continuous-martingale-version]].
The filtration is assumed to satisfy the usual conditions, as required by the
cited local-integrability definition. Choose the progressively measurable
versions constructed in step 1.1 for these integrals and for the finite-energy
integrals below. Continuity means continuity on a measurable probability-one
event, and indistinguishability means equality at all times on such an event,
as in that continuous-version theorem. Local square integrability and the
canonical energy bounds are almost-sure assertions.

1. **Existence.** There is an adapted process $M=(M_t)_{t\ge0}$ with continuous
   paths, called the **localized Ito integral** $H\cdot B$, such that for every
   $n$ the stopped process $M^{\tau_n}$ is indistinguishable from $M^{(n)}$.
   Consequently $M$ is a continuous local martingale relative to
   $(\mathcal F_t)$ with localizing sequence $(\tau_n)$, and for every
   $n$ and $t$
   $$EM_{t\wedge\tau_n}^2=EA_{t\wedge\tau_n}\le n .$$

2. **Characterization.** If $N$ is an adapted process with continuous paths and
   $N_0=0$ such that $N^{\tau_n}$ is indistinguishable from $M^{(n)}$ for every
   $n$, then $N$ is indistinguishable from $M$. In particular $M$ is the unique
   continuous local martingale, up to indistinguishability, whose stopped
   finite-energy integrals are the $M^{(n)}$.

3. **Independence of the localizing sequence.** Let $(\rho_k)$ be a
   nondecreasing sequence of stopping times with $\rho_k\uparrow\infty$ almost
   surely and $E\int_0^tH_s^21_{(0,\rho_k]}(s)\,ds<\infty$ for all $k$ and all
   finite $t$, and let $N$ be an adapted process with continuous paths and
   $N_0=0$ such that $N^{\rho_k}$ is indistinguishable from the finite-energy
   integral of $H1_{(0,\rho_k]}$ for every $k$. Then $N$ is indistinguishable
   from $M$.

4. **Stopping identity for finite-energy integrands.** If $G$ is a predictable
   process with $E\int_0^TG^2ds<\infty$ and $G\cdot B$ denotes its continuous
   version [[thm-ito-integral-process-has-a-continuous-martingale-version]],
   with the same progressive version convention (extending $G$ by zero after $T$), then for every stopping time $\sigma$ and every $0\le t\le T$
   $$(G\cdot B)_{t\wedge\sigma}=\int_0^tG_s1_{(0,\sigma]}(s)\,dB_s\qquad\text{almost surely},$$
   and the two sides are continuous processes on $[0,T]$, hence
   indistinguishable there. A global identity follows by applying this clause
   on each finite horizon when $G$ has finite energy on every finite horizon.
   This clause is the finite-energy stopping identity used by item 17.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $H$ be a locally
square-integrable predictable process
[[def-locally-square-integrable-predictable-brownian-integrand]] with localized
integral $H\cdot B$ in the progressively measurable version of
[[thm-localized-ito-integral]], with its measurable-full-event convention
for indistinguishability. The filtration satisfies the usual conditions and
local energy is finite almost surely on every finite horizon, as required by
the local-integrability definition. Let $\tau$ be a
stopping time [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]]. Then the process
$s\mapsto(H\cdot B)_{s\wedge\tau}$ and the localized integral of the process
$1_{[0,\tau]}H$ are indistinguishable:
$$(H\cdot B)_{t\wedge\tau}=\int_0^t1_{[0,\tau]}(s)H_s\,dB_s\qquad\text{for every }t\ge0\text{, up to indistinguishability}.$$
In particular, for $H$ of finite energy this reduces to the stopping identity
of [[thm-localized-ito-integral]], and for $\tau\equiv\infty$ it is the
definition of the localized integral.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $H$ be a predictable
process with $E\int_0^TH_s^2ds<\infty$ for every finite $T$. Then there is an
adapted process $M=(M_t)_{t\ge0}$ with continuous paths such that
$M_t=\int_0^tH_s\,dB_s$ almost surely for every $t\ge0$
[[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]], and $M$ is a
square-integrable martingale relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$
[[def-continuous-time-adapted-process-and-martingale]]: $EM_t^2=E\int_0^tH_s^2ds<\infty$
for every $t$. Any two such continuous versions agree at every time on one
measurable event of probability one; in particular the continuous version is
unique in this common-full-measure-event sense, and it is the only continuous
square-integrable martingale whose value at each deterministic $t$ is the
integral class.

This conclusion is deliberately distinguished from the exact definition of
indistinguishability in
[[def-law-modification-and-indistinguishability-of-processes]]. On a
noncomplete probability space the full equality set, although it contains the
measurable probability-one event constructed below, need not itself be
measurable. On a complete probability space the two notions coincide, because
the complement of the equality set is then a measurable subset of a null set.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Fix $T>0$. For predictable
$H,K$ with finite energy $E\int_0^TH^2ds,E\int_0^TK^2ds<\infty$ the integrals
$\int_0^TH\,dB$ of
[[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]] satisfy
$$\int_0^T(H+K)\,dB=\int_0^TH\,dB+\int_0^TK\,dB,\qquad \int_0^T(aH)\,dB=a\int_0^TH\,dB\quad(a\in\mathbb R),$$
and the identities are equalities of $L^2(P)$-classes (almost sure
equalities). Moreover the map $H\mapsto\int_0^TH\,dB$ is an isometry,
$$E\Bigl(\int_0^TH\,dB\Bigr)^2=E\int_0^TH^2ds=\|H\|^2_{L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)},$$
it takes values in the mean-zero subspace of $L^2(P)$, and the bilinear cross
identity
$$E\Bigl[\Bigl(\int_0^TH\,dB\Bigr)\Bigl(\int_0^TK\,dB\Bigr)\Bigr]=E\int_0^TH_sK_s\,ds$$
holds for all such $H,K$. In particular the image of the map is a closed
subspace of $L^2(P)$ isometric to the predictable $L^2$ space of $H$'s, and
$H\mapsto\int_0^TH\,dB$ is injective up to the $(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$-class.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $m,d\ge1$ be finite
integers, let $B=(B^1,\dots,B^m)$ be a standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion,
and let $X$ be an $\mathbb R^d$-valued continuous Brownian Ito process
$$X^i_t=X^i_0+\int_0^tb^i_s\,ds+\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s, \qquad i=1,\dots,d,$$
in the sense of [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], including its usual-filtration and almost-sure coefficient-integrability conventions. Let
$f\in C^{1,2}([0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^d)$, meaning that $f,\partial_tf$,
$\partial_if$ and $\partial_i\partial_jf$ ($1\le i,j\le d$) exist and are
continuous. Then, up to indistinguishability, for every $t\ge0$
$$f(t,X_t)=f(0,X_0)+\int_0^t\Bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\Bigr)(s,X_s)\,ds+\sum_{i,k}\int_0^t\partial_if(s,X_s)\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s,$$
For the displayed integrands, intersect the measurable full events of continuity and the decomposition of $X$, and of coefficient integrability at all integer horizons. Its null complement belongs to $\mathcal F_0$ under the usual conditions. Set $X,X_0,b,\sigma$ to zero there. These representatives preserve all coefficient classes and the decomposition up to indistinguishability, with everywhere continuous $X$ and everywhere locally finite coefficient path integrals. All displayed integrands use these representatives.

The stochastic integrals are localized Ito integrals of the predictable
locally square-integrable integrands $\partial_if(\cdot,X)\sigma^{ik}$, and
$(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}_s=\sum_k\sigma^{ik}_s\sigma^{jk}_s$. In
differential form,
$df(t,X_t)=\bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\bigr)(t,X_t)\,dt+\sum_{i,k}\partial_if(t,X_t)\sigma^{ik}_t\,dB^k_t$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$ and let
$M=(M^1,\dots,M^d)$ be an adapted $\mathbb R^d$-valued process with continuous
paths such that every coordinate $M^i$ is a real continuous local martingale
relative to $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$ in the sense of
[[def-continuous-time-adapted-process-and-martingale]]. Suppose $M_0=0$ almost surely and
whose quadratic covariations in the sense of
[[def-quadratic-covariation-of-brownian-ito-processes]] satisfy
$[M^i,M^j]_t=\delta_{ij}t$ for all $i,j$ and all $t\ge0$. Then $M$ is a
standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion [[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]],
and for all $0\le s<t$ the vector increment $M_t-M_s$ is independent of
$\mathcal F_s$ with law $N_d(0,(t-s)I_d)$.

Assume AC for the supplied existence theorem. Write $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ for the unique class in $L^1(\Omega,\mathcal G,P|_{\mathcal G})$ consisting of conditional-expectation versions of $X$. A chosen real $\mathcal G$-measurable representative is a **version**. Equalities and inequalities involving these classes mean almost-sure equalities and inequalities.

Existence is [[thm-conditional-expectation-exists-by-radon-nikodym]] and uniqueness is [[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]], applied to [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. The quotient is [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. If $X=X^{\ast}$ almost surely, [[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]] gives identical event integrals, so the output class is independent of the input representative. The [[def-axiom-of-choice]] assumption is inherited from RN existence.

Assume AC for existence. For real $X,Y\in L^1(P)$ and $a,b\in\mathbb R$, $E[aX+bY\mid\mathcal G]=aE[X\mid\mathcal G]+bE[Y\mid\mathcal G]$. Conditional expectation is positive, preserves order and constants, satisfies $E(E[X\mid\mathcal G])=EX$, and $|E[X\mid\mathcal G]|\le E[|X|\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. Also $X<Y$ almost surely implies $E[X\mid\mathcal G]<E[Y\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely.

Assume AC for existence. If $\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ and $X\in L^1(P)$, then $E[E[X\mid\mathcal G]\mid\mathcal H]=E[X\mid\mathcal H]$ and $E[E[X\mid\mathcal H]\mid\mathcal G]=E[X\mid\mathcal H]$ almost surely. Also, if a version of $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ is $\mathcal H$-measurable, it is a version of $E[X\mid\mathcal H]$.
Assume AC. For fixed real $X\in L^1(P)$, the classes $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$, as $\mathcal G$ ranges over all sub-sigma-algebras of $\mathcal F$, form a uniformly integrable family.

If $X_n\to X$ in probability and $\{X_n:n\in\mathbb N\}$ is uniformly
integrable, then $X\in L^1(\mathbb P)$ and $X_n\to X$ in $L^1$.

Assume AC. If $M$ is a martingale and $\sigma\le\tau$ are stopping times bounded by a deterministic $N$, then
$$\mathbb E[M_\tau\mid\mathcal F_\sigma]=M_\sigma\quad\text{a.s.},$$
so $\mathbb EM_\tau=\mathbb EM_\sigma$. For a submartingale $X$ the conditional and expectation inequalities point upward; for a supermartingale they point downward.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $H$ be a predictable
process on $[0,T]$, where $T\ge0$, with $E\int_0^TH_s^2ds<\infty$. Extend $H$ by zero after $T$ when applying the global continuous-version theorem, and let
$M_t=\int_0^tH_s\,dB_s$ be the continuous version of
[[thm-ito-integral-process-has-a-continuous-martingale-version]]. Then
$$E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|M_t|^2\le4\,E\int_0^TH_s^2\,ds .$$
The left-hand side is finite and does not depend on the chosen version, since
any two continuous versions are indistinguishable. Every continuous version of
the integral process satisfies the same bound. The path supremum in this
expectation means its measurable version $S_D=\sup_{q\in D}|M_q|$ on the
countable scaled dyadic grid $D$ (including both endpoints). Continuity
identifies it with the path supremum on a measurable event of probability one.
Indistinguishability here uses that full-event convention, as in the cited
continuous-version theorem, without assuming completeness of the filtration.

Assume the data and hypotheses of
[[def-ito-sde-and-strong-solution]] on $[0,T]$, with $T\ge0$, finite
dimensions $d,m\ge1$, Lipschitz constant $L$, and linear-growth constant
$K$. There is a strong solution $X$ on the given filtered probability space.
It is unique up to indistinguishability among strong solutions with the same
initial value and Brownian driver, and it satisfies
$$E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|X_t|^2\le(1+3E|X_0|^2)e^{C_TT},\qquad C_T:=6K^2T+24mK^2.$$
The bound is independent of any later numerical mesh.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space with a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$, and let $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ be a real process
that satisfies $X_t:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable for every $t\ge0$, and has
continuous paths, in the strong sense that $s\mapsto X_s(\omega)$ is continuous
on $[0,\infty)$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$. Then $X$ is progressively
measurable and predictable relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ in the sense of
[[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]], including at time
zero under the generator convention $\{0\}\times A$, $A\in\mathcal F_0$. No
choice principle is used. Here a filtration means an increasing family of
sub-sigma-algebras of $\mathcal F$. The fixed-time measurability hypothesis
is the adaptedness terminology of clause 1 of
[[def-continuous-time-adapted-process-and-martingale]]; only that clause is
used, not its conditional-expectation or martingale interface and its Choice
assumption.

If instead the paths are continuous only on an event $A\in\mathcal F$ with
$P(A)=1$, the conclusion holds for the modification that is set equal to $0$
off $A$ provided $A\in\mathcal F_0$; without such a measurability assumption on
the continuity event no predictability claim is made, because predictability
is a property of the given joint map.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Let
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space with a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. All processes here
are real-valued and indexed by $[0,\infty)$. AC is inherited from the cited
continuous-time-filtration interface, whose separate martingale clause uses
conditional expectation. Once the filtered probability space and stopping
times are given, the progressive and predictable constructions below make no
additional choice: they use only generated sigma-algebras and product
rectangles.

1. **Progressively measurable.** A process $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **progressively measurable** relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when for every
   $t\ge0$ the restricted map
   $[0,t]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$, $(s,\omega)\mapsto X_s(\omega)$, is
   measurable for the product sigma-algebra
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$
   [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]].

2. **Time-zero and interval generators.** On the product space
   $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$, let $\mathcal P$ be the sigma-algebra generated by
   the family
   $$\mathcal G:=\bigl\{(s,u]\times A:\ 0\le s<u<\infty,\ A\in\mathcal F_s\bigr\}\ \cup\ \bigl\{\{0\}\times A:\ A\in\mathcal F_0\bigr\}.$$
   The interval generators with $s=0$ are included, so $(0,u]\times A$ with
   $A\in\mathcal F_0$ is a generator. The sigma-algebra $\mathcal P$ exists by
   [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]] and is called the
   **predictable sigma-algebra**. A process $H=(H_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **predictable** when the map $(s,\omega)\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is
   $\mathcal P$-measurable. For a finite horizon $T>0$ we write
   $\mathcal P_T$ for the sigma-algebra on $[0,T]\times\Omega$ generated by the
   same family restricted to $u\le T$ together with the time-zero generators;
   this is the trace of $\mathcal P$ on $[0,T]\times\Omega$. Indeed, the
   trace of an interval generator is empty when $s\ge T$, and otherwise is
   $(s,\min(u,T)]\times A$, while time-zero generators are unchanged.
   Conversely every listed finite-horizon generator is such a trace.

3. **Sections, adaptedness, and null sets.** Two structural conventions are
   used repeatedly and are part of the definition.
   (a) Every generator is a measurable rectangle of
   $\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$, hence
   $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$; the time-zero
   generator $\{0\}\times A$ has $dt\otimes P$-measure zero for every $A$. A
   set in $\mathcal P$ has its section at each fixed time $s$ in $\mathcal F_s$:
   sets with that section property form a sigma-algebra, and each generator
   has the property by the increasing-filtration condition. Its section at
   each fixed $\omega$ is Borel in time, by the same sigma-algebra argument.
   (b) If a process is predictable then it is progressively measurable: for
   $s\le t$ the section $\omega\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is $\mathcal F_s$-measurable
   $\subseteq\mathcal F_t$-measurable, and the progressive-measurability claim
   is the restriction of the joint map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$; the restriction
   of a $\mathcal P$-measurable map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$ is measurable for
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$ because every generator with $u\le t$
   lies in that product sigma-algebra and the generators with $u>t$ have
   intersection with $[0,t]\times\Omega$ of the form $(s,t]\times A$ with
   $s<t$ and $A\in\mathcal F_s$, or the empty set when $s\ge t$.
   The time-zero generators also lie in
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$.

The family $\mathcal G$ need not itself contain the whole space, but a finite intersection
of generators is empty or again a generator, or a time-zero generator, because
$(s,u]\cap(s',u']=(s\vee s',u\wedge u']$ and $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_{s\vee s'}$
whenever $A\in\mathcal F_s$, $A'\in\mathcal F_{s'}$, while
$\{0\}\times A$ is disjoint from every interval generator, including
$(0,u]\times A'$. Two time-zero generators intersect in
$\{0\}\times(A\cap A')$ with $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_0$.
Thus the family consisting of the whole space
together with finite intersections of generators is a pi-system generating
$\mathcal P$; this is the structural fact used by the density theorem below.

Because predictability is a measurability requirement for the joint map, it is
preserved by pointwise limits, products and linear combinations of predictable
processes. A deterministic function $h$ of time defines a predictable process
exactly when $h$ is Borel measurable: the sets $C$ for which
$C\times\Omega\in\mathcal P$ form a sigma-algebra containing the intervals
$(s,u]$ and $\{0\}$, hence all Borel sets. Conversely, take any fixed
$\omega\in\Omega$ (a probability space is nonempty) and use the Borel
time-section property from 3(a) on every inverse image of an open set.
This single choice uses no choice axiom. In particular the
indicators $1_{[0,u]}$ and $1_{(0,u]}$ are predictable for every deterministic
$u\ge0$, and the process $s\mapsto 1_{s\le\tau(\omega)}$ for a stopping time
$\tau$ [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] is predictable, since
$$\{(s,\omega):s>\tau(\omega)\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}(q,\infty)\times\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}\bigcup_{n>q}(q,n]\times\{\tau<q\}$$
is a countable union of generators: for rational $q>0$ one has
$\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q'<q,\ q'\in\mathbb Q}\{\tau\le q'\}\in\mathcal F_q$. The
complement of that set inside $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$ is the event of the
indicator, so $1_{[0,\tau]}$ is predictable; its left-continuity in the time
variable is the visual form of the same computation.

No completeness of the filtration and no right continuity of $(\mathcal F_t)$
is used or assumed. Apart from the inherited ambient assumption just recorded,
the constructions in this definition are choice-free.

Let $(f_n)$ be nonnegative measurable functions. Then
$$\int \liminf_{n\to\infty}f_n\,d\mu\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int f_n\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mu$ be a positive measure and let $
u$ be a signed measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. Assume there is an increasing measurable exhaustion $(X_n)$ with $ igcup_nX_n=X$, $\mu(X_n)<+\infty$, and $|
u|(X_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$. If $
u\ll\mu$, then there exists a measurable real-valued function $f$, unique up to $\mu$-almost-everywhere equality, such that
$$
u(E)=\int_Ef\,d\mu\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$
If in addition $|
u|(X)<+\infty$, then $f\in L^1(\mu)$.

Assume AC and let $P_0,P_1$ be probability measures on one measurable space.
Let $r$ be a nonnegative measurable representative of the likelihood-ratio
class for $P_1$ versus $P_0$. If $P_1\ll P_0$, then
$$
E_{P_0}[g r]=E_{P_1}[g]
$$
for every nonnegative measurable $g$, and also for every real-valued
$P_1$-integrable measurable $g$. Here $E_{P_i}[h]$ means
$\int h\,dP_i$. Without $P_1\ll P_0$, this identity need not hold because the
singular component may be nonzero.

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Put $C=C([0,\infty),\mathbb R)$, give $C$ the uniform-on-compacts topology,
and write $\pi_t(f)=f(t)$. Then
$$\mathcal B(C)=\sigma(\pi_t:t\ge0)=\sigma(\pi_q:q\in\mathbb Q\cap[0,\infty)).$$
Here each expression on the right denotes the smallest sigma-algebra on $C$
making every displayed coordinate map measurable. No choice principle is used.

derivations.claim: By [F1], applied to $f(m,a)=e^{m-a/2}$, $dZ_t=Z_t\theta_t\cdot dW_t$. Stopping at integer levels of $A$, $|M|$ and $Z$ makes the integral finite-energy, so $Z$ is a positive continuous local martingale. All these stops tend beyond every time strictly less than $T$, and stabilize at $T$, because the paths and energy are bounded on $[0,T]$. A nonnegative local martingale $N$ is a supermartingale: Fatou first gives integrability, and conditional Fatou gives $E[N_t\mid\mathcal F_s]\le\liminf_jE[N_{t\wedge\rho_j}\mid\mathcal F_s]=\liminf_jN_{s\wedge\rho_j}=N_s$ for a localizing sequence. The conditional Fatou assertion follows by taking the increasing infima of the tails, using conditional order and monotone convergence; conditional monotone convergence follows by ordinary monotone convergence in the defining event integrals. Thus $E Z_t\le1$, and the same assertion applies to the stopped exponential for every scalar multiple of $\theta$.

We record the continuous stopping consequence needed below. Let $V$ be a continuous true martingale on $[0,T]$. For $\rho\le T$, round $\rho$ upward to stopping times $\rho_j$ on finite grids whose meshes tend to zero. Discrete bounded optional sampling in [F3] gives $V_{\rho_j}=E[V_T\mid\mathcal F_{\rho_j}]$. This family is UI and converges almost surely to $V_\rho$, hence in $L^1$. If $A\in\mathcal F_\rho$, then $A\in\mathcal F_{\rho_j}$, as is checked by the defining stopped-event tests, so passage in those tests gives $V_\rho=E[V_T\mid\mathcal F_\rho]$. In particular the family of all $V_\rho$, $\rho\le T$, is UI. Stopping preserves true martingality: for fixed $s<t$, choose the grids on $[0,t]$ to contain $s$; the finite-grid identity $E[1_AV_{t\wedge\rho_j}]=E[1_AV_{s\wedge\rho_j}]$ for $A\in\mathcal F_s$ follows by telescoping grid increments with the left-endpoint measurable stopping indicators. Continuity and the preceding UI argument pass it to $V^\rho$. Thus both continuous stopping facts used below have been derived from the discrete supplier.

To prove data processing, write $r=dR/dS$, and let $u$ be the density of $F_\#R$ relative to $F_\#S$; absolute continuity follows immediately by taking inverse images of null sets. Testing events in $\sigma(F)$ gives $u\circ F=E_S[r\mid\sigma(F)]$. If $D(R\|S)=\infty$ the desired inequality is immediate. Otherwise $\phi(r)$ is integrable, where $\phi(x)=x\log x$ on $x>0$ and $\phi(0)=0$, since its negative part is bounded by $1/e$. For positive rational $a$, the tangent line $\ell_a(x)=(1+\log a)x-a$ lies below $\phi(x)$ on $x\ge0$, by differentiating their difference, and $\phi(x)=\sup_{a\in\mathbb Q,\ a>0}\ell_a(x)$, including $x=0$ by $a\downarrow0$. Conditional order gives $\ell_a(E_S[r\mid\sigma(F)])\le E_S[\phi(r)\mid\sigma(F)]$. Intersect these countably many full events, take the supremum and then expectations. This yields $D(F_\#R\|F_\#S)\le D(R\|S)$, with left integrability following from the lower bound $-1/e$ and the displayed conditional upper bound.

If $A_T\le n$, then at every stopping time $\rho\le T$, $Z_\rho^2=\exp(2M_\rho-2A_\rho)\exp(A_\rho)$, whence $E Z_\rho^2\le e^n$ by step 1.1 applied to the stopped integrand $2\theta1_{[0,\rho]}$. Apply this bound to localizing stops for $Z$. Their terminal values are UI, since their tail integrals are at most $e^n/R$ above level $R$. They converge almost surely, and hence in $L^1$, to $Z_T$. The same holds at every earlier time, so passage in martingale event tests proves true martingality. In particular $Z_t=E[Z_T\mid\mathcal F_t]$.

Suppose $Z$ is true and put $Q=Z_TP$. Since $0<Z_T<\infty$ almost surely, these probabilities are equivalent. For $A\in\mathcal F_t$, $Q(A)=E_P[Z_T1_A]=E_P[Z_t1_A]$ by [F3], so $Q|\mathcal F_t=Z_tP|\mathcal F_t$; at $t=0$ this is $Q|\mathcal F_0=P|\mathcal F_0$. The measures have identical null sets, so completeness and the usual filtration conditions persist. Let $B=W-\int\theta ds$, whose drift has finite total variation by pathwise Cauchy–Schwarz. For a coordinate $i$, let $\sigma_r$ be the first time $|B^i|$ reaches $r$, capped at $T$. These are stopping times because continuous adapted path suprema are measurable by their rational-time suprema. Product Itô gives $$d(Z_tB^i_{t\wedge\sigma_r})=Z_t1_{[0,\sigma_r]}(t)dW_t^i+B^i_{t\wedge\sigma_r}Z_t\theta_t\cdot dW_t.$$ The finite-variation terms cancel against $d[Z,W^i]_t=Z_t\theta_t^idt$. The right side is locally square integrable, so the product is a $P$-local martingale.

For every $\rho\le T$, $|Z_\rho B^i_{\rho\wedge\sigma_r}|\le rZ_\rho$. By step 1.2, $Z_\rho=E[Z_T\mid\mathcal F_\rho]$, and these random variables form a UI family. Hence the localizing stopped products in step 2.2 are UI. Passing their event tests in $L^1$ makes $ZB^{i,\sigma_r}$ a true $P$-martingale. For $A\in\mathcal F_s$, change of measure at times $s,t$ now gives $E_Q[1_AB^i_{t\wedge\sigma_r}]=E_P[1_AZ_tB^i_{t\wedge\sigma_r}]=E_P[1_AZ_sB^i_{s\wedge\sigma_r}]=E_Q[1_AB^i_{s\wedge\sigma_r}]$. Thus $B^i$ is a $Q$-local martingale. Its localizers increase to the horizon because continuous paths are bounded on each compact interval.

If $E_PA_T<\infty$, [F1] gives $E_PM_T=0$ and $E_PM_T^2=E_PA_T$. Since $dQ/dP=Z_T>0$, $dP/dQ=1/Z_T$ and $-\log Z_T=-M_T+A_T/2$ is $P$-integrable. The definition of relative entropy therefore gives $D(P\|Q)=E_P[-\log Z_T]=E_PA_T/2$. This establishes the asserted identity whenever $Z$ is true; it does not yet presume true martingality in the unbounded-energy sufficient condition.

Subtracting a continuous finite-variation path preserves quadratic covariations: its squared-increment sum is at most its largest increment times its total variation, and its mixed-increment sum with $W^i$ is at most the largest Brownian increment times that variation. Both errors tend to zero pathwise along every vanishing-mesh partition. The Brownian covariation limits also hold in $Q$-probability: $P(E_n)\to0$ implies $Q(E_n)=E_P[Z_T1_{E_n}]\to0$ by integrability of $Z_T$. Consequently $[B^i,B^j]_t=\delta_{ij}t$ under $Q$, and [F2] proves that $B$ is $Q$-Brownian. The cited proof applies on $[0,T]$ because it uses only finite pairs of times. Equivalently, if the Brownian space is defined for all times, set $\theta=0$ after $T$ and keep $Z$ constant; the argument applies on every horizon and uses [F2] literally. A space defined only up to $T$ can first be extended by an independent Brownian continuation.

Consider that sufficient condition. The three candidate drifts are predictable by [F5] and obey $|v_t(X)|\le K(1+\sup_{u\le t}|X_u|)$ for some common $K$. The base Brownian and Euler equations are explicit, and the diffusion equation is covered by [F4]. Their solutions have finite second path moment: for Euler this follows immediately from its finite recursion and the Brownian maximal bound. Pathwise boundedness gives $A_T<\infty$. Set $\tau_n=\inf\{t:A_t\ge n\}\wedge T$ and $Z^n_t=\exp(M_{t\wedge\tau_n}-A_{t\wedge\tau_n}/2)$. By step 2.1 it is a true martingale. Under $Q_n=Z^n_TP$, step 4.1 gives Brownian motion $B^n=W-\int_0^{\cdot\wedge\tau_n}\theta_sds$, and substitution in the additive equation gives $$dX_t=\bigl(1_{[0,\tau_n]}(t)c_t(X)+1_{(\tau_n,T]}(t)a_t(X)\bigr)dt+\sqrt2dB^n_t.$$ The initial law is unchanged and the switched drift obeys the same $K$ bound.

Uniformly in $n$, $$E_{Q_n}\sup_{t\le T}|X_t|^2\le C_T:=(1+3E|X_0|^2+24dT)e^{6K^2T^2}-1.$$ To establish finiteness without assuming it, first stop $X$ at its first exit from a ball of radius $R$. If $|X_0|\ge R$ the stop is zero and the stopped path is $X_0$, which retains its integrable second moment. Before stopping, the drift bound uses the corresponding stopped path supremum. Cauchy–Schwarz, $|x+y+z|^2\le3(|x|^2+|y|^2+|z|^2)$, and [F4] therefore bound its expected squared supremum $q_{n,R}(t)$ by $3E|X_0|^2+24dT+6K^2T\int_0^t(1+q_{n,R}(s))ds$. These quantities are finite for fixed $R$. Put $H(t)=1+3E|X_0|^2+24dT+6K^2T\int_0^t(1+q_{n,R}(s))ds$; then $1+q_{n,R}\le H$ and $H'\le6K^2TH$ almost everywhere, so the integrating factor gives $q_{n,R}(T)\le C_T$. The ball stops tend to $T$ on every bounded continuous path; Fatou proves the displayed bound.

For the integrands used here, elementary left-endpoint sums on deterministic partitions refining the Euler grid give the identity $$M_{T\wedge\tau_n}=\int_0^T1_{[0,\tau_n]}(s)\theta_s\cdot dB_s^n+A_{T\wedge\tau_n}.$$ Here is a direct justification across the measure change. All path coefficients are continuous on each of finitely many open mesh intervals; multiplying by the stopping indicator adds at most one discontinuity. Stop further on bounded path and coefficient levels. Their left-endpoint staircases converge for almost every time on each path, are bounded, and hence converge in predictable $L^2$ under both equivalent measures by dominated convergence. Both Brownian integrals converge by their respective isometries, while the drift integral converges by Cauchy–Schwarz. For each elementary sum the identity follows by substituting $dW=dB^n+1_{[0,\tau_n]}\theta ds$. Equivalence identifies the probability limits; removing the extra increasing stops proves the displayed identity. The $Q_n$-Brownian integral has mean zero since its energy is at most $n$. As $|\theta_t|^2\le4K^2(1+\sup_{u\le t}|X_u|^2)$, step 6.1 yields $$E_P[Z^n_T\log Z^n_T]=\tfrac12E_{Q_n}A_{T\wedge\tau_n}\le2K^2T(1+C_T).$$

Since $z\log z\ge-1/e$, step 7.1 gives, for $R>1$, $E_P[Z^n_T1_{\{Z^n_T>R\}}]\le(2K^2T(1+C_T)+1/e)/\log R$. Thus $(Z^n_T)$ is UI. On every path with $A_T<\infty$, $\tau_n=T$ for all sufficiently large $n$, so $Z^n_T\to Z_T$ almost surely and in $L^1$. In particular $E Z_T=1$. Step 1.1 gives a supermartingale with initial mean one and terminal mean one, so every intermediate mean equals one; the nonnegative conditional supermartingale deficit has mean zero, proving true martingality of $Z$. Apply step 4.1 without stops to get the target equation. The base finite second path moment in step 5.1 and the coefficient bound imply $E_PA_T<\infty$, so step 3.2 applies.

The target path law is uniquely determined, as follows. For target zero it is $X_0+\sqrt2B$; for Euler target it is the finite mesh recursion, a Borel function of $(X_0,B)$. For target $b(X_t)$, use the Picard recursion $X^{m+1}=X_0+\int_0^{\cdot}b(X_s^m)ds+\sqrt2B$ starting with $X^0_t=X_0$. Its iterates are Borel functions on $\mathbb R^d\times C([0,T],\mathbb R^d)$: integration of a continuous path is a uniform limit of its deterministic Riemann sums. For every fixed input $(x,w)$, put $C=T|b(x)|+\sqrt2\sup|w|$. The first iterate difference has supremum at most $C$, and induction in the Lipschitz integral inequality bounds the $m$th difference up to time $t$ by $CL^{m-1}t^{m-1}/(m-1)!$. Their uniformly summable majorant proves uniform convergence for every continuous input. The limit is consequently a Borel function of that input. The deterministic Lipschitz integral inequality makes any solution with the same input agree with this limit: if $h(t)$ is the path supremum of their difference, $h(t)\le L\int_0^th(s)ds$, and the integrating factor forces $h=0$. Under the changed measure, $B$ has Wiener law and is independent of $X_0$, because its future increments are independent of $\mathcal F_0$; independence of the entire path follows first on finite-time cylinder events and then on their generated Borel sigma-algebra by [F7]. Thus $(X_0,B)$ has the same product law on every such space, and its Borel solution map proves the asserted uniqueness in law.

If $\theta=0$, then $Z=1$, $Q=P$ and the entropy is zero. A zero mesh interval is omitted; the stated grid has strictly positive lengths, and no lower bound on those lengths is needed. At time zero all integrals vanish and the initial law is preserved. The excluded horizon $T=0$ has the same trivial conclusions. AC has exactly the inherited uses in [A1].

Assume AC. Let $T>0$, let $W$ be a standard $d$-dimensional Brownian
motion on a complete usual filtered probability space, with increments after
$s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$, and let $\theta$ be predictable with
$A_T:=\int_0^T|\theta_s|^2ds<\infty$ almost surely. Set
$$M_t=\int_0^t\theta_s\cdot dW_s,\qquad A_t=\int_0^t|\theta_s|^2ds,\qquad Z_t=\exp(M_t-A_t/2).$$
If $Z$ is a true martingale on $[0,T]$, then $Q=Z_TP$ is equivalent to $P$,
its restriction to $\mathcal F_0$ equals that of $P$, and
$$B_t=W_t-\int_0^t\theta_sds$$
is standard Brownian motion under $Q$ relative to the same filtration.
If $A_T$ is bounded by a deterministic constant, $Z$ is a true martingale.
If additionally $E_PA_T<\infty$, then
$$D(P\|Q)=\frac12E_PA_T.$$

Here is a sufficient condition that permits unbounded $A_T$. Fix a globally
Lipschitz vector field $b:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$, a finite deterministic
grid $0=t_0<\cdots<t_N=T$, and $\eta(t)=t_k$ for
$t_k\le t<t_{k+1}$. Let each of the two path drifts $a,c$ be one of
$0$, $b(X_t)$, or $b(X_{\eta(t)})$. Suppose
$$X_t=X_0+\int_0^ta_s(X)ds+\sqrt2W_t,\qquad E|X_0|^2<\infty,$$
where $X_0$ is $\mathcal F_0$-measurable. For
$\theta_t=(c_t(X)-a_t(X))/\sqrt2$, the exponential $Z$ above is a true
martingale, and under $Q$ the process $X$ has the unique path law with
initial law $\mathcal L_P(X_0)$ and drift $c$ and dispersion $\sqrt2I_d$.
Moreover $E_PA_T<\infty$, so the entropy identity applies. Values of the
piecewise coefficients at grid points do not affect any integral.

Finally, for any probability measures $R\ll S$ and measurable statistic
$F$, relative entropy decreases under pushforward:
$$D(F_\#R\|F_\#S)\le D(R\|S).$$
All equivalence and entropy assertions concern this finite horizon.

Assume the data and hypotheses of
[[def-ito-sde-and-strong-solution]] on $[0,T]$, with $T\ge0$, finite
dimensions $d,m\ge1$, Lipschitz constant $L$, and linear-growth constant
$K$. There is a strong solution $X$ on the given filtered probability space.
It is unique up to indistinguishability among strong solutions with the same
initial value and Brownian driver, and it satisfies
$$E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|X_t|^2\le(1+3E|X_0|^2)e^{C_TT},\qquad C_T:=6K^2T+24mK^2.$$
The bound is independent of any later numerical mesh.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $H$ be a predictable
process on $[0,T]$, where $T\ge0$, with $E\int_0^TH_s^2ds<\infty$. Extend $H$ by zero after $T$ when applying the global continuous-version theorem, and let
$M_t=\int_0^tH_s\,dB_s$ be the continuous version of
[[thm-ito-integral-process-has-a-continuous-martingale-version]]. Then
$$E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|M_t|^2\le4\,E\int_0^TH_s^2\,ds .$$
The left-hand side is finite and does not depend on the chosen version, since
any two continuous versions are indistinguishable. Every continuous version of
the integral process satisfies the same bound. The path supremum in this
expectation means its measurable version $S_D=\sup_{q\in D}|M_q|$ on the
countable scaled dyadic grid $D$ (including both endpoints). Continuity
identifies it with the path supremum on a measurable event of probability one.
Indistinguishability here uses that full-event convention, as in the cited
continuous-version theorem, without assuming completeness of the filtration.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Fix $T>0$. For predictable
$H,K$ with finite energy $E\int_0^TH^2ds,E\int_0^TK^2ds<\infty$ the integrals
$\int_0^TH\,dB$ of
[[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]] satisfy
$$\int_0^T(H+K)\,dB=\int_0^TH\,dB+\int_0^TK\,dB,\qquad \int_0^T(aH)\,dB=a\int_0^TH\,dB\quad(a\in\mathbb R),$$
and the identities are equalities of $L^2(P)$-classes (almost sure
equalities). Moreover the map $H\mapsto\int_0^TH\,dB$ is an isometry,
$$E\Bigl(\int_0^TH\,dB\Bigr)^2=E\int_0^TH^2ds=\|H\|^2_{L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)},$$
it takes values in the mean-zero subspace of $L^2(P)$, and the bilinear cross
identity
$$E\Bigl[\Bigl(\int_0^TH\,dB\Bigr)\Bigl(\int_0^TK\,dB\Bigr)\Bigr]=E\int_0^TH_sK_s\,ds$$
holds for all such $H,K$. In particular the image of the map is a closed
subspace of $L^2(P)$ isometric to the predictable $L^2$ space of $H$'s, and
$H\mapsto\int_0^TH\,dB$ is injective up to the $(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$-class.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer. An
$\mathbb R^d$-valued process $B=(B_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **standard
$d$-dimensional Brownian motion** if:

1. $B_0=0$ almost surely;
2. for every finite list $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n$, the vector increments
   $$B_{t_j}-B_{t_{j-1}},\qquad 1\le j\le n,$$
   are mutually independent and have laws
   $N_d(0,(t_j-t_{j-1})I_d)$; and
3. there is one measurable event $A$ with $P(A)=1$ such that
   $t\mapsto B_t(\omega)$ is continuous from $[0,\infty)$ to
   $\mathbb R^d$ for every $\omega\in A$.

Equivalently, its $d$ coordinate processes $B^\alpha=(B_t^\alpha)_{t\ge0}$
are independent standard one-dimensional Brownian motions. Here independence
of the processes means the following precise assertion. Put
$I=[0,\infty)$ and equip $\mathbb R^I$ with its cylinder sigma-algebra. The
maps
$$ \Phi_\alpha:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathbb R^I, \qquad \Phi_\alpha(\omega)(t)=B_t^\alpha(\omega), \qquad 1\le\alpha\le d, $$
are independent random elements.

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

Assume AC and let $P_0,P_1$ be probability measures on one measurable space.
Let $r$ be a nonnegative measurable representative of the likelihood-ratio
class for $P_1$ versus $P_0$. If $P_1\ll P_0$, then
$$
E_{P_0}[g r]=E_{P_1}[g]
$$
for every nonnegative measurable $g$, and also for every real-valued
$P_1$-integrable measurable $g$. Here $E_{P_i}[h]$ means

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.
